stories.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after 20 years
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Uganda first deployed its troops to Somalia in 2007 By Swaibu Ibrahim ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kampala Â and Â Basillioh Rukanga Published 2 November 2026, 08:40 GMT Updated 2 hours ago Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country. Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time. He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal. Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), which was established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants. A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.

"Journalists are increasingly paying with their lives for reporting from the frontlines of war and far too often those responsible for their killings are not held accountable," said Director-General Khaled El-Enany. UNESCO first began measuring the proportion of journalist killings that go unpunished in 2012. The rate reached 86 per cent in 2024-2025, up one per cent from the previous two-year period. A confirmed total of 189 journalists and other media workers lost their lives in 2024-2025, or 20 per cent more than during the previous biennium and the highest number since 2014-2015. stories.title: Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown
stories.summary: Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown Gillian Parker/VOA A Patriotic Front supporter proudly displays his identification and voter cards, Lusaka, Zambia (file photo). 1 November 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) Opposition and Critics Forcibly Disappeared, Arbitrary Detained, Beaten Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members, lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August. The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices. The authorities should immediately halt the crackdown, allow access to lawyers and medical care to detainees, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses. (Johannesburg) - The Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities have also yet to credibly explain or investigate the killing of an opposition leader in contested circumstances. "Zambia's government should break this dangerous cycle of repression," said Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz , deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch. "The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces." Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines President Hakainde Hichilema was reelected in the August 13 election, which observers said was marred by irregularities such as a suspension of counting and limited fundamental freedoms . En juin dernier, le service central des recherches judiciaires de la gendarmerie camerounaise annonce avoir démantelé un réseau fonctionnant sur ce modèle. 13 personnes sont arrêtées et plus de 600 victimes identifiées, enrôlées de force dans des maisons à Douala, Bafoussam, Ebolowa, Kye-Ossi, Bertoua, Ngaoundéré, Maroua, Garoua et Yaoundé, et obligées à leur tour d'attirer de nouvelles proies. Des arnaqués obligés à escroquer d'autres personnes Le système pyramidal est connu : les premiers trafiquants se font passer pour des recruteurs, utilisent les réseaux sociaux pour diffuser des offres d'emplois et des opportunités d'études à l'étranger, facturent des frais de recrutement, attirent leurs victimes et les séquestrent dans des concessions transformées en dortoirs collectifs, où, selon la gendarmerie, elles subissent une pression constante pour piéger leurs proches. Dans son rapport, l'Observatoire du crime organisé et de la violence en Afrique centrale de l'Institute for Security Studies (ISS) pointe la dimension transnationale de cette criminalité, avec des commanditaires en Asie (Malaisie) et des ramifications en Afrique de l'Ouest et en Afrique centrale.

Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. stories.summary: Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books View image in fullscreen Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books Obituary Roy Moxham obituary My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India , a country he visited many times on extended trips. His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company. Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.

But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa , meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear". Photograph: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP/Getty Images UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’ Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days. A year after the fall of El Fasher , the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city. A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze .
